title: Predicting Participant Compliance With Fitness Tracker Wearing and Ecological Momentary Assessment Protocols in Information Workers: Observational Study

summary.oneLiner: Demographics and personality explain a modest share of wearable and survey compliance, but compliance in a study's second week predicts far more.
summary.overview: Studies that use wearables or short in-the-moment phone surveys (ecological momentary assessments, or EMAs) lose value when participants stop complying. This observational study gave 757 information workers fitness trackers for a year and EMAs for their first 56 days, then tested how well compliance could be predicted in advance. Demographics and personality explained 16% (EMA) and 25% (wearable) of the variation in compliance in a held-out sample; adding second-week compliance raised this to 62% and 66%. Being older, a native English speaker, a previous wearable owner and conscientious were associated with higher compliance, while extraversion and holding a supervisory role were associated with lower compliance. The authors recommend running a two-week pilot to spot participants at risk of dropping off, among other practices.
summary.question: To what extent can participants' compliance with wearable and survey protocols be predicted from their individual characteristics and early compliance?
summary.method: Observational study. Thirty-one individual and behavioural variables were considered and 14 selected for beta regression models predicting EMA compliance at 56 days and wearable compliance at one year, evaluated on a held-out sample. A survey about study participation was correlated with compliance.
summary.data: 757 information workers given fitness trackers for one year, with EMAs in their first 56 days; demographics, personality and early behaviour such as use of the study portal.
findings: Demographics and personality explained 16% of the variance in EMA compliance and 25% in wearable compliance in a held-out sample.

Higher compliance was associated with being older, speaking English as a first language, having owned a wearable before and conscientiousness; lower compliance with extraversion and a supervisory role.
Higher wearable compliance was also negatively associated with agreeableness and neuroticism.
Adding second-week compliance explained 62% (EMA) and 66% (wearable) of the variance.

Compliance correlated with participants' views on ease of participation, the usefulness of the compliance portal, timely issue resolution and adequate pay, which the authors suggest are levers for improving it.
summary.whyItMatters: For anyone running wearable programmes or long panel studies, the authors recommend a two-week pilot to measure trait-like compliance, oversampling by participant characteristics to avoid bias when non-compliers are dropped, an issue-tracking portal, and careful troubleshooting support.
